subject: Agriculture
title: The Population Bomb Fear
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Population Bomb Fear.

hook.text: In 1968, Paul Ehrlich predicted hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s. The world panicked.

buildup.text: World population was doubling every 35 years. Food production wasn't keeping pace—or so it seemed.

discovery.text: Ehrlich's dire predictions sparked global urgency. Governments poured money into agricultural research.

twist.text: The mass famine never came. A scientific revolution was already underway—one Ehrlich hadn't accounted for.

climax.text: The Green Revolution would prove that science could outrun population growth—at least for a while.

punchline.text: The prediction was wrong. The panic it caused was useful.

quiz.question: What did Paul Ehrlich predict in 'The Population Bomb'?
options: Mass starvation in the 1970s from population growth

details.summary: Paul Ehrlich's 1968 book 'The Population Bomb' predicted mass famine by the 1970s as population growth outpaced food production. This topic covers the fear that drove the Green Revolution, why Ehrlich's predictions were wrong, and the debates that continue about population and food supply.

faq.question: What did Paul Ehrlich predict in The Population Bomb?
faq.answer: Ehrlich argued that exponential population growth would inevitably outstrip food production, leading to mass starvation by the 1970s-80s. He advocated for drastic population control measures and predicted that no amount of agricultural technology could save hundreds of millions from famine.

faq.question: Why were Ehrlich's famine predictions wrong?
faq.answer: Ehrlich underestimated agricultural science. The Green Revolution's high-yield crop varieties, synthetic fertilizers, and irrigation dramatically increased food production. Global food output more than doubled while population grew, and the share of people in poverty and hunger declined sharply.
